lessons.try_it: You have a 1 ms control-loop task, a 100 ms sensor task, and a background logging task. Assign priorities using rate-monotonic reasoning and predict what happens when the control task's computation grows from 200 us to 900 us.

lessons.title: IPC: Queues, Semaphores, and Event Flags
concepts: Queues move data between tasks safely: the RTOS copies the item, so sender and receiver never share memory. Size the queue for burst depth, not average rate.
Binary semaphores signal events (ISR to task: data ready); counting semaphores manage resource pools (3 DMA channels free); mutexes guard shared resources and carry priority inheritance.
Never use a binary semaphore as a mutex: semaphores have no owner and no priority inheritance — a classic source of priority inversion bugs that mutexes solve.
Event flags (or task notifications) are the lightweight path: a 32-bit flag word per task with zero queue overhead — ideal for ISR-to-task signaling when no data payload is needed.

example.code:
xQueueSend(xSensorQ, &sample, pdMS_TO_TICKS(10)); /* task->task, copies */
xSemaphoreGiveFromISR(xDataReady, &woke);          /* ISR->task signal */
portYIELD_FROM_ISR(woke);                          /* switch if higher prio woke */
xSemaphoreTake(xSpiMutex, portMAX_DELAY);          /* own the bus */
example.walkthrough: Four IPC idioms in four lines. The queue send copies the sample — the sender's buffer can be reused immediately. The ISR gives a semaphore and records whether a higher-priority task woke; portYIELD_FROM_ISR requests an immediate context switch so the woken task runs without waiting for the next tick. The mutex take blocks until the SPI bus is free — and because it is a mutex, not a semaphore, priority inheritance protects against inversion while holding it.

pitfalls: Blocking inside an ISR: FromISR APIs never block — passing a timeout to an ISR API either asserts or corrupts. ISRs signal; tasks wait.
Queue of pointers instead of data: sending &local through a queue shares a stack address that dies when the sender returns. Copy the data or use a static pool.
Forgetting portYIELD_FROM_ISR: the woken high-priority task waits until the next tick — adding up to a full tick of latency to your real-time response.
lessons.try_it: Design the IPC for an ISR that fires at 1 kHz with 16-bit samples: choose between a queue, a direct-to-task notification, and a double buffer. Justify your pick on latency, RAM, and ISR time.

lessons.title: Priority Inversion and Priority Inheritance
concepts: Priority inversion: a high-priority task blocks on a resource held by a low-priority task, which is then preempted by a medium-priority task — the high-priority task effectively waits on the medium one. Mars Pathfinder famously hit this.

Priority inheritance fixes it: when a high-priority task blocks on a mutex, the holder temporarily inherits the high priority — the medium task can no longer preempt it, so the resource is released quickly.
Inheritance only applies to mutexes, not semaphores: another reason to use the right primitive. It also does not fix unbounded blocking from long critical sections — keep them short.
The interview answer has three parts: name the scenario (H waits on L, M preempts L), name the fix (priority inheritance or priority ceiling), and name the residual risk (chained blocking).

example.code:
WITHOUT inheritance:                  WITH inheritance:
  H(p3) blocks on mutex held by L(p1)   H(p3) blocks -> L inherits p3
  M(p2) preempts L -> L stalls          M(p2) cannot preempt (L now p3)
  H waits on M's whole timeslice        L finishes, drops to p1, H runs
  -- unbounded delay                    -- bounded by L's critical section
example.walkthrough: The left timeline is the bug: H needs the mutex but L holds it, and M — which does not even want the mutex — preempts L indefinitely, so H's delay is unbounded. The right timeline is the fix: the moment H blocks, L's priority is raised to H's level, M can no longer preempt, L finishes its critical section fast and releases the mutex, H runs. The key interview phrase is bounded blocking: inheritance converts an unbounded delay into one bounded by the longest critical section.

pitfalls: Reaching for inheritance when the real fix is design: if H and L constantly contend, restructure so they do not share — lock-free queues or separate resources beat clever protocols.
Priority ceiling confusion: the ceiling protocol raises the holder to the max priority of any potential user immediately (no waiting for contention). Know both names — interviewers ask.
Inheritance across multiple mutexes: chained blocking can still deadlock. Keep lock ordering strict and nesting shallow.
lessons.try_it: Draw the three-task inversion timeline for your own system: identify one real mutex, name the H/M/L tasks, and compute the worst-case blocking time with and without inheritance.

lessons.title: MMIO: Talking to Hardware Through Memory
concepts: Memory-mapped I/O: peripheral registers appear at fixed addresses in the CPU's address space. Reading and writing those addresses IS operating the hardware — there is no special I/O instruction on ARM.
Bit manipulation is the daily idiom: set, clear, and toggle individual bits with masks — REG |= BIT; REG &= ~BIT — the read-modify-write pattern you will use constantly.

Register maps come from the datasheet: every peripheral chapter lists offsets, reset values, and bit fields. The vendor header turns these into structs — verify the struct against the datasheet before trusting it.
Write-only and clear-on-read registers break naive read-modify-write: status registers that clear on read, or write-1-to-clear bits, need exact access patterns — always read the access-type column.

example.code:
#define GPIOA_ODR (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x48000014)
#define PIN5      (1u << 5)
GPIOA_ODR |= PIN5;    /* set pin 5 high */
GPIOA_ODR &= ~PIN5;   /* set pin 5 low */
/* write-1-to-clear status: NEVER read-modify-write */
#define USART_ISR (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x4001381C)
USART_ISR = (1u << 6);   /* clear TC flag by writing 1 */
example.walkthrough: The first block is classic MMIO: a macro types the output data register address as volatile uint32_t, and bit 5 is set and cleared with masks — neighboring pins undisturbed. The second block shows the trap: the USART status register uses write-1-to-clear semantics, so USART_ISR |= (1u << 6) would read the register (possibly clearing other flags as a side effect) and write back stale bits. The correct pattern is a plain assignment of exactly the bits to clear.

pitfalls: Read-modify-write on write-1-to-clear registers: you clear flags you never intended to touch. Match the access pattern to the access type.
Missing volatile on the register macro: the compiler optimizes your carefully sequenced writes into one — or zero — actual bus transactions.
Trusting the vendor header blindly: headers have shipped with wrong offsets. Cross-check the first register you touch against the datasheet.
lessons.try_it: Pick a peripheral on your target (for example a timer). Write the macros and init sequence to enable its clock, set a prescaler, and start it — citing the datasheet register names.

lessons.title: Interrupts: From Pin Wiggle to ISR
concepts: The interrupt path: peripheral asserts, the NVIC prioritizes, the CPU finishes the current instruction, stacks registers, jumps to the vector table entry — your ISR runs — return restores context.
ISRs must be short and non-blocking: acknowledge the peripheral, move data to a buffer or signal a task, exit. Anything longer belongs in a task — the ISR is the most expensive context in the system.

Interrupt priorities need a plan: group them (0 = safety-critical, mid = comms, low = housekeeping), and keep RTOS-aware ISRs at or below the RTOS's max-syscall priority so they can call FromISR APIs.
Shared data between ISR and main code is the classic race: declare it volatile, keep accesses atomic-width, or guard with a brief interrupt disable — and document which.

example.walkthrough: The ISR checks the receive-not-empty flag first — never assume why you were called. Reading RDR both grabs the byte and clears the flag (peripheral-specific: know your clear mechanism). The byte goes to a queue via the FromISR variant, which cannot block. After servicing, portYIELD_FROM_ISR switches to the woken task immediately if it outranks the interrupted one. The NVIC lines set a mid-level priority and enable the interrupt — priority and enable are separate steps, and forgetting the enable is a rite of passage.

pitfalls: Forgetting to clear the interrupt source: the ISR exits, the pending flag is still set, and you re-enter instantly — a livelock that looks like a hang.
Calling blocking or non-FromISR RTOS APIs in an ISR: asserts in debug, corruption in release. The FromISR suffix exists for a reason.
Priority misconfiguration: an ISR above the RTOS syscall priority calling FromISR APIs corrupts the kernel. Draw your priority map before writing ISRs.
lessons.try_it: Write the ISR skeleton for a timer that fires every 1 ms: clear the update flag, increment a volatile tick counter, and signal a task every 1000 ticks. List every line that could go wrong.

lessons.title: DMA: Moving Data Without the CPU
concepts: DMA moves data between peripherals and memory while the CPU does other work: configure source, destination, size, and trigger — the DMA engine handles the transfers and interrupts on completion.
The classic use is streaming: ADC samples to RAM buffer, or RAM buffer to UART/SPI transmit, at rates the CPU could never sustain with per-byte interrupts.

Cache coherency is the DMA trap on cached cores: the CPU cache may hold stale data the DMA just wrote (invalidate before the CPU reads) or dirty data the DMA has not seen (clean before the DMA reads).
Double buffering (ping-pong) keeps streams continuous: DMA fills buffer A while the CPU processes buffer B, then they swap — no gaps, no overruns, bounded latency.

example.walkthrough: The DMA is configured to move ADC data-register reads into a 256-sample buffer in circular mode — when it reaches the end it wraps automatically, so the stream never stops. Half-transfer and full-transfer interrupts split the buffer into two 128-sample halves: while the DMA fills one half, the CPU processes the other. This is the ping-pong pattern — continuous acquisition with zero CPU per-sample cost and deterministic processing windows.

pitfalls: Cache incoherency: DMA wrote fresh samples but the CPU reads stale cache lines. On cached cores, invalidate the buffer region before reading — this bug is intermittent and maddening.
Buffer alignment and burst rules: DMA engines often require word-aligned buffers and transfer sizes that are multiples of the burst width. Misaligned buffers cause silent truncation.
Forgetting the DMA interrupt enable or flag clear: the transfer completes once and never again — or the ISR re-fires forever. Same discipline as peripheral ISRs.
lessons.try_it: Size a double-buffered DMA scheme for a 10 kHz sensor stream where processing takes up to 8 ms per half-buffer: pick buffer sizes, compute worst-case latency, and state where cache maintenance goes.

lessons.title: Device Trees: Describing Hardware to Software
concepts: A device tree is a data structure describing the hardware: which peripherals exist, their addresses, interrupts, clocks, and pin connections — so one driver build supports many boards.

Nodes, properties, and phandles: each peripheral is a node with properties (reg = address/size, interrupts = IRQ numbers, clocks = clock sources). Phandles reference other nodes, wiring the description together.
Overlays customize per board: the base tree describes the SoC; an overlay adds the board's specific wiring (which I2C bus the sensor is on, which GPIO is the LED) without forking the base.
In interviews, device trees test whether you separate mechanism from description: the driver is generic code; the tree is board-specific data. Hardcoding addresses in drivers is the anti-pattern.

example.walkthrough: This node describes a temperature sensor at I2C address 0x48. compatible binds it to the generic tmp117 driver — the driver matches on this string, not on board-specific code. The interrupt properties say its alert pin connects to GPIO1 pin 17, falling edge. vcc-supply phandles the 3.3 V regulator node, so the driver framework can power the sensor up and down. Change boards? Write a new overlay remapping these properties — the driver never changes.

pitfalls: Address-cells and size-cells mismatches: parent and child disagreeing on cell counts silently decodes the wrong address. The most common device-tree boot failure.
compatible string typos: the driver never binds, the device never probes, and nothing logs an error — just silence. Triple-check against the driver source.
Assuming device trees are Linux-only: Zephyr and modern RTOS board support use the same model. The concept — data-driven hardware description — transfers everywhere.
lessons.try_it: Write a device-tree node for an SPI flash on spi1, chip-select GPIO2 pin 3, 16 MHz max speed. Then explain what changes if the board moves it to spi2.

lessons.title: Atomicity on Bare Metal: Read-Modify-Write Hazards
concepts: Atomic means indivisible as observed: on a 32-bit core, aligned 32-bit loads and stores are atomic — but read-modify-write sequences (count++) are three operations and an ISR can land between them.
The lost-update bug: main reads count (5), the ISR fires and increments to 6, main writes back 6 — one increment is lost. It happens rarely, which is why it ships to customers.
Critical sections (brief interrupt disable) make short sequences atomic: disable, do the read-modify-write, re-enable. Keep them under a few microseconds or you break real-time guarantees.
On multi-core or with DMA, interrupt disable is not enough: you need hardware atomic primitives (exclusive access, or atomic builtins) because the other agent is not stopped by your interrupt mask.

example.walkthrough: This function atomically snapshots and clears a shared flag. It saves the current interrupt state first — blindly re-enabling interrupts on exit would break a caller that already had them disabled (nested critical sections). Between disable and enable, the read and the clear are indivisible: no ISR can interleave. The function returns the old value so the caller knows what happened. Save-and-restore discipline is what separates a correct critical section from a latent bug.

pitfalls: Critical sections that grow: what starts as just this counter accumulates logging and queue sends, and suddenly your 2 us section is 200 us and the 1 kHz ISR misses.
Forgetting to restore PRIMASK on every exit path: an early return inside a critical section with interrupts still disabled freezes the system's timing.
Using interrupt disable for DMA-shared data on cached cores: the DMA engine does not care about your PRIMASK. Pair with cache maintenance or use non-cacheable memory.
lessons.try_it: Find three shared variables in a typical sensor node (ISR tick counter, main-loop command flag, DMA buffer index). For each, state the writer(s), reader(s), and the minimal correct protection.

lessons.title: Lock-Free Patterns: Ring Buffers and Single-Writer Queues
concepts: A single-producer single-consumer (SPSC) ring buffer needs no locks: the producer owns the write index, the consumer owns the read index, and each index is only written by its owner.
Power-of-two size with a mask replaces modulo: idx & (SIZE-1) compiles to one AND instruction — fast enough for ISRs, and it keeps the wrap logic branchless.
Memory ordering matters: the data write must be visible before the index update. On Cortex-M (strongly ordered) a compiler barrier suffices; on weaker architectures you need explicit barriers.
Full vs empty disambiguation: keep one slot permanently empty (full when (wr+1)&mask == rd), or maintain a separate count. The wasted slot is cheaper than the ambiguity bug.

example.walkthrough: The ISR (producer) computes the next write index with a mask — no modulo, no branch. If it equals the read index the buffer is full, and the ISR drops the byte: blocking or overwriting inside an ISR is worse than dropping. The data byte is stored, then a data-memory barrier ensures the byte is visible before the index update — otherwise the consumer could read a stale slot. Finally wr advances. The task (consumer) mirrors this with rd. Each index has exactly one writer, so no lock is needed — that single-writer invariant is the whole trick.

pitfalls: Two writers: the SPSC invariant breaks the moment a second ISR or the main loop also writes. One producer means one — audit every write to wr.
Forgetting volatile on the indices: the consumer's loop caches rd and never sees new data. Volatile (plus barriers) on shared indices is mandatory.
Using the ring buffer across cores without barriers: Cortex-M single-core habits do not transfer to dual-core parts — add the architecture's barrier instructions.
lessons.try_it: Write rb_get (the consumer side) mirroring rb_put. Then answer: what breaks if the consumer also wants to peek without consuming? Design the minimal extension.

lessons.title: ISRs and the Main Loop: Deferred Work and Flags
concepts: The ISR/main-loop split is the simplest concurrency model: the ISR does the minimum (capture, timestamp, set flag), and the main loop does the work. Most bare-metal firmware is exactly this.
Flags must be volatile and cleared carefully: read-and-clear atomically or you lose events that arrive between the read and the clear.
Event groups scale the pattern: one 32-bit word where each bit is an event source — the main loop waits on any-bit-set instead of polling N flags, and ISRs set bits with atomic OR.
Know when to graduate: when deferred work needs priorities, timeouts, or blocking, the flag pattern has hit its limit — that is the signal to bring in an RTOS.

example.walkthrough: The timer ISR clears its source flag first (avoiding re-entry), then sets a bit in the shared events word with an atomic OR — the only ISR-side operation. The main loop snapshots and clears the whole word atomically, then dispatches on the bits: no polling, no missed events, because the snapshot captured everything pending. __WFI puts the CPU to sleep until the next interrupt — the loop consumes zero power and zero CPU while idle. This is the superloop done right: event-driven, low-power, and race-free.

pitfalls: Non-atomic read-modify-clear of the events word: an ISR setting a bit between your read and clear loses the event. Snapshot-and-clear must be one critical section.
__WFI races: an event set between checking events and executing WFI sleeps until the next interrupt. Check-then-sleep needs care — use the SEV/WFE pattern.
Letting the ISR grow: just one more line turns the ISR into the application. If the ISR is longer than about 20 lines, the work belongs in the main loop.
lessons.try_it: Extend the pattern with a sensor data-ready ISR that also queues one byte. Show where the byte goes (hint: not in the events word) and how the main loop retrieves it without racing the ISR.

lessons.title: Data Races: Finding and Fixing Shared-State Bugs
concepts: A data race is two unsynchronized accesses to the same memory with at least one write: ISR vs main, task vs task, DMA vs CPU. The symptom is intermittent corruption — the hardest bug class to reproduce.
Reproduction strategy: stress the timing (flood the ISR, shrink delays), instrument with trace (which access happened when), and suspect every non-volatile, non-guarded shared variable.

The fix menu, in order of preference: eliminate sharing (copy data, do not share it), make access atomic (single aligned word), use lock-free patterns (SPSC ring), guard with a critical section or mutex.
Interviewers want the war-story structure: symptom, hypothesis, how you proved it (trace or logic analyzer), the fix, and how you prevented recurrence (assert, review checklist).

example.code:
/* RACY:                              FIXED:
   ISR:  speed = new_val;               ISR:  speed = new_val;  // atomic word
   main: if (speed > LIM) ...           main: uint32_t s = speed; // snapshot once
   main: use(speed); // may differ      main: if (s > LIM) use(s); // consistent
*/
example.walkthrough: The racy version reads the shared variable twice: the ISR can update it between the comparison and the use, so main acts on a value that failed the check — or passes a check on a stale value. The fix snapshots once into a local: every subsequent use sees the same value. The ISR's single aligned word store is atomic by hardware, so the snapshot is always a real value, never a torn half-old half-new mix. One local variable, one read — the cheapest race fix there is.

pitfalls: Reading a multi-word struct without protection: a 64-bit timestamp on a 32-bit core tears — the ISR updates the high word between your two reads. Snapshot under a critical section.
Assuming it works on my board means correct: races depend on timing that changes with optimization level, temperature, and silicon revision. -O0 hiding a race is not a fix.
Fixing with a bigger hammer than needed: a mutex around a single word read adds priority-inversion risk where a snapshot sufficed. Match the fix to the sharing shape.
lessons.try_it: Audit this snippet for races: an ISR increments ticks (uint32_t) and sets ready=1; main loops while(!ready); t=ticks; ready=0;. List every race and rewrite it correctly.

lessons.title: JTAG and SWD: The Debug Wire
concepts: JTAG/SWD is your lifeline to a dead board: it halts the CPU, reads and writes memory and registers, sets breakpoints, and flashes firmware — all without any working software on the target.
SWD (Serial Wire Debug) is the modern two-pin standard for ARM: SWDIO plus SWCLK plus ground. JTAG's four-plus pins survive mainly on larger parts and boundary scan.
Semihosting and ITM/SWO give you printf without a UART: ITM channels stream trace data over the debug probe — invaluable when the board's serial port is already in use.
Security fuses change the game: readback protection can disable the debug port on production parts. Know your part's protection levels before you lock yourself out.

example.code:
(gdb) target extended-remote :3333   # OpenOCD
(gdb) monitor reset halt
(gdb) break main
(gdb) continue
(gdb) info registers
(gdb) x/16wx 0x20000000              # dump 16 words of RAM
example.walkthrough: This GDB session via OpenOCD is the bring-up ritual: connect to the probe, halt the CPU out of reset (before it can run off into the weeds), break at main, and run. info registers shows the CPU state — check the stack pointer first; a garbage SP means your vector table or linker script is wrong. The memory dump verifies RAM contents. When a board does nothing, this sequence tells you in thirty seconds whether the CPU is alive, where it is, and what the stack looks like.

pitfalls: SWD wiring mistakes: swapped SWDIO/SWCLK, missing ground, or NRST held low — the probe reports no device found and the board is actually fine. Check wiring before suspecting silicon.
Debug probe speed: the default clock may be too fast for a board with long traces or a slow clock config. Drop the adapter speed before declaring the chip dead.
Leaving semihosting enabled in release: a semihosting breakpoint with no debugger attached hangs the firmware. Gate it behind a debug build flag.
lessons.try_it: With a probe connected, halt at reset, dump the first 16 words at the vector table address, and decode: initial SP, reset handler address. Verify both against your linker script.

lessons.title: Logic Analyzers: Seeing Signals in Time
concepts: A logic analyzer captures digital signals over time: it answers what actually happened on the wire when the protocol misbehaves — clock stretching, missing ACKs, wrong baud rates all become visible.
Sample rate rule: capture at 4-10x the fastest signal of interest. Debugging 400 kHz I2C wants at least a few MHz of sample rate; SPI at 20 MHz wants 100+ MHz.

Protocol decoders turn wiggles into bytes: most analyzers decode UART/SPI/I2C/CAN in software — you read transactions, not edges. Always verify the decoder's settings (baud, polarity, bit order) match the bus.
Triggering is the skill: trigger on the anomaly (a NACK, a missing edge, a specific address) rather than capturing blindly — the interesting event is usually one in a million.

example.code:
# sigrok decoders from the command line — scriptable captures
sigrok-cli -d fx2lafw --samples 1000000 --time 100 \
  -P i2c:sda=0:scl=1 -A i2c=address-data
# output: START 0x48+W ACK 0x2A ACK ... NACK STOP
example.walkthrough: This sigrok command captures one second with a low-cost FX2-based analyzer and runs the I2C decoder on channels 0 and 1. The annotation output reads like a transaction log: START, address 0x48 with write bit, ACK, data byte 0x2A, ACK — and the tell-tale NACK before STOP that explains the failed transfer. Scriptable captures beat GUI clicking for regression: save the command, re-run it after every driver change, diff the output.

pitfalls: Ground clips: a floating or long ground lead adds noise that looks like signal integrity problems. Short ground, close to the signal under test.
Decoder misconfiguration: wrong baud rate decodes garbage that looks like a firmware bug. Verify the decoder against a known-good transaction first.
Forgetting the analyzer loads the bus: cheap analyzers add capacitance — a marginal I2C bus that works without the probe and fails with it is telling you about rise times, not firmware.
lessons.try_it: Capture your UART TX at 115200 with a decoder. Measure the actual bit time from the capture and compute the real baud rate — compare against the configured value and explain any error.

lessons.title: Fault Handlers: Catching HardFaults with Dignity
concepts: A HardFault is the CPU's last resort: unaligned access, invalid address, bus error, or escalated lesser faults. The default handler is an infinite loop — replace it with one that captures forensic state.
The stacked frame is the goldmine: on exception entry the CPU pushes R0-R3, R12, LR, PC, xPSR. Your handler receives the stack pointer and can decode exactly which instruction faulted and why.
The fault status registers name the cause: precise vs imprecise bus errors, unaligned access, divide-by-zero, invalid state — read them before you guess.
Ship the handler in production: log the fault record to retained RAM or flash, then reset. Field failures with no fault record are undebuggable; with one, they are routine.

example.walkthrough: The assembly stub figures out which stack was active when the fault hit: bit 2 of LR tells whether the handler used the main or process stack, and it passes that stack pointer to the C function. The C handler indexes the stacked frame — sp[6] is the program counter at the fault, sp[5] the link register — and reads the fault status register for the cause. It logs the record to flash and resets. Next boot, your startup code can report the fault PC and cause instead of silence.

pitfalls: Infinite-loop default handlers in production: the device bricks in the field with zero information. A forensic handler costs 50 lines and pays for itself once.
Forgetting the FPU stacked frame: with lazy FPU stacking the frame layout differs — your sp[6] indexing is wrong on FPU faults. Handle both frame sizes.
Logging to flash inside the fault handler without care: if the fault was a bus error on the flash controller, your logging faults recursively. Keep a RAM-first record.
lessons.try_it: Deliberately cause a HardFault (write to an unmapped address), capture the stacked PC, and use objdump to find the exact faulting instruction. Verify the fault status register names the cause you expected.

lessons.title: Post-Mortem Debugging: Crash Dumps Without a Debugger
concepts: Post-mortem debugging answers field failures: the device crashed with no probe attached — what can you still learn? Retained RAM, flash logs, and fault records are your witnesses.
Design the crash record up front: fault registers, stacked PC/LR, a rolling event log (last N events with timestamps), task states, and a boot counter. Size it once; it serves every future bug.
Watchdog resets are crash data too: log the watchdog bite with the same event log — watchdog at tick 48291, last event: sensor task blocked on queue points straight at the deadlock.
Reproduce from the record: the crash dump plus the firmware build (keep every released ELF) lets you decode addresses offline with addr2line — no hardware needed.

example.walkthrough: This struct is the flight-data recorder: it lives in a noinit RAM section that startup code deliberately does not zero, so it survives software resets. The magic word distinguishes a real record from garbage after power loss. The rolling event log is the timeline — the last 32 significant events before the crash, each an event ID plus tick. Combined with the fault PC decoded via addr2line against the exact released ELF, you reconstruct the crash offline: what happened, in what order, in which task.

pitfalls: noinit RAM vs power loss: retained RAM survives reset but not power cycles — document that, and mirror critical records to flash for true persistence.
Not keeping release ELFs: a crash PC is meaningless without the exact binary's symbol table. Archive the ELF with every release — it costs kilobytes.
Event log without timestamps: sensor read failed 32 times tells you nothing; sensor read failed at tick 48290, watchdog at 48291 tells you everything.
lessons.try_it: Define the 8 most valuable event IDs for your sensor node, implement the rolling log macro (2 lines per event), and prove the record survives a software reset.

lessons.title: Bring-Up Order: Clock Tree, GPIO, UART First
concepts: Bring-up order is risk order: clock tree first (nothing works without clocks), then GPIO (blink an LED — your first proof of life), then UART (your debug console for everything after).
The clock tree is the foundation: source selection, dividers, and peripheral clock gates. A peripheral with its clock gate off is dead silicon — the number one my-driver-doesn't-work cause.
GPIO proof-of-life: configure one pin as output and toggle it in a loop. If the LED blinks, your toolchain, flash, clock, and GPIO all work — four unknowns eliminated in one test.
UART console next: printf-style output turns every subsequent bring-up step from guesswork into observable behavior. Bring-up without a console is debugging blindfolded.

example.code:
/* bring-up sequence — each step verified before the next */
clock_init();          /* HSE 8MHz -> PLL -> 168MHz sysclk */
gpio_init(LED_PIN);    /* proof of life */
blink_forever();       /* VERIFY: LED blinks at 1Hz */
uart_init(115200);     /* debug console */
printf("clocks ok, gpio ok\r\n");  /* VERIFY: text on console */
example.walkthrough: This is the first-day script for any new board: clocks, GPIO, blink, UART, print. Each line is followed by a physical verification — the LED, the serial terminal — before proceeding. The discipline is no unverified step: if the LED does not blink, you debug clocks and GPIO now, not after writing the sensor driver. The UART print is the moment bring-up becomes efficient — from here on, every subsystem announces its own status.

pitfalls: Starting with the complex peripheral: writing the sensor driver before the UART console means debugging the sensor with no visibility. Boring first, fancy later.
Assuming default clock config is correct: reset defaults are usually the slow internal oscillator — your baud rates and timings are all wrong until you configure the tree.
No verification between steps: stacking five untested init calls then wondering which failed wastes hours. Verify each, commit each.
lessons.try_it: Write the bring-up checklist for a new board: list each step, its verification method, and the single most likely failure at that step.

lessons.title: Sensor Integration: From Datasheet to Live Data
concepts: Datasheet-first integration: power sequencing, I2C/SPI address and timing, register map, and the exact init sequence — implement the datasheet's flowchart before writing clever code.
Verify communication before functionality: read the WHO_AM_I / chip-ID register first. The right ID means your bus, addressing, and timing all work; wrong data means stop and debug the bus.
Polling first, interrupts later: get correct data with simple polling reads, then add data-ready interrupts and DMA. Each layer is verified before the next complicates it.
Sanity-check the physics: does the temperature read near room temp? Does the accelerometer read about 1g on Z when flat? Data that violates physics is a driver bug until proven otherwise.

example.walkthrough: The integration ritual in code: read the chip ID and assert it — this single check validates the entire bus path. Run the datasheet's init sequence exactly as documented. Take a blocking read, convert with the datasheet's LSB weight (never a magic number — comment the source), and assert the result is physically plausible. Each ASSERT is a tripwire: when integration breaks later, the first failing assert names the layer.

pitfalls: Skipping the WHO_AM_I check: debugging wrong temperature values for hours when the bus was never working. The ID read is the cheapest test you have.
Magic numbers for conversion: raw * 0.0078 with no comment rots — the next reader cannot verify it. Cite the datasheet section for every scale factor.
Interrupts before polling works: adding the data-ready ISR to a driver that never produced correct polled data doubles the debug surface. Layer by layer.
lessons.try_it: Pick a real sensor datasheet. Extract: the WHO_AM_I register and expected value, the init sequence steps, and the conversion formula with its datasheet citation.

lessons.title: RTOS Integration: Tasks, Watchdog, and Supervision
concepts: Task decomposition for the sensor node: sensor task (acquire), processing task (filter/convert), comms task (transmit), supervisor task (watchdog + health). Each blocks on its inputs; none busy-waits.
The watchdog is a supervision contract: each task checks in (I am alive and making progress) on its own cadence; the supervisor task pets the hardware watchdog only if all check-ins are fresh.
Check-ins must prove progress, not just liveness: a task stuck in a loop still runs. Check in after completing real work units (samples processed, packets sent) with sequence numbers.
Degraded modes beat dead devices: if the sensor task stops checking in, the supervisor can reset just that task or drop to a safe mode — design the recovery before you need it.

example.walkthrough: The supervisor task is the system's immune system: every 500 ms it checks each task's last check-in timestamp against that task's timeout. Only if every task is fresh does it pet the hardware watchdog — a stuck task therefore triggers a watchdog reset even though the supervisor itself is healthy. On failure it enters a safe mode and logs which task failed, so the post-mortem record names the culprit. Timeouts are per-task because a 1 kHz control task and a 0.1 Hz logging task have very different healthy cadences.

pitfalls: Petting the watchdog from a timer ISR: the watchdog then proves only that interrupts work — a deadlocked task set never triggers it. Pet only on verified task health.
One timeout for all tasks: too tight and healthy slow tasks false-trigger; too loose and fast failures go undetected. Per-task timeouts from measured cadence.
No safe mode: watchdog reset as the only recovery loses in-flight state and looks unprofessional in a demo. Design degraded operation first.
lessons.try_it: Define check-in points and timeouts for your three tasks. Then describe the exact safe-mode behavior when the comms task stops checking in but sensors are healthy.

lessons.title: Power Profiling: Proving the Power Budget
concepts: Power budgets are contracts: two years on a coin cell decomposes into sleep current times sleep time plus active current times active time. Measure each term — do not estimate from datasheets alone.
Measure with the right tool: a multimeter averages (hiding spikes); a current profiler or shunt plus scope shows the real waveform — radio TX spikes lasting microseconds dominate some budgets.
Profile by subsystem: measure sleep current with each peripheral's clock gated, then enable them one at a time. The delta names the hog — usually a forgotten clock gate or a floating input pin.
The demo artifact is the spreadsheet: measured sleep/active currents, duty cycles, computed lifetime, and the margin. Interviewers trust measured numbers; they discount datasheet math.

example.code:
/* power budget: CR2032 = 220 mAh */
sleep_uA   = 3.2;    /* measured, all gated, RTC on */
active_mA  = 18.5;   /* measured, sensor+radio burst */
active_ms  = 120;    /* per 10 s cycle */
avg_uA = (3.2*9880 + 18500*120) / 10000;  /* approx 225 uA */
life_h = 220000 / 225;                     /* approx 978 h */
example.walkthrough: The budget math is simple; the measurements are the work. Sleep current was measured at 3.2 uA with everything gated except the RTC — that number comes from the profiler, not the datasheet. Each 10-second cycle spends 120 ms active at 18.5 mA (sensor read plus radio burst, measured). The weighted average is about 225 uA, giving roughly 978 hours from a 220 mAh cell — about 40 days. The honest conclusion is 40 days, not 2 years — exactly the kind of measured truth that earns trust, plus a clear optimization target.

pitfalls: Datasheet-only budgets: typical values at 25C with ideal config. Your firmware's actual sleep current is what ships — measure it.
Floating inputs: an unconfigured GPIO floats, and the input buffer draws shoot-through current — often microamps per pin, dwarfing your careful sleep modes.
Forgetting the debug probe: a connected debugger keeps clocks and peripherals alive. Always profile with the probe disconnected.
lessons.try_it: Build the budget spreadsheet for your node: list every power state, its measured current, its duty cycle, and the computed lifetime. Highlight the single biggest term — that is your optimization target.

lessons.title: The Embedded Interview Arc: What They're Really Testing
concepts: Embedded interviews test four layers: C fluency (pointers, volatile, bit manipulation), systems thinking (memory, concurrency, hardware), debugging discipline (how you attack the unknown), and communication (can you explain it clearly).

Every question is a proxy: explain volatile tests whether you have fought the optimizer; design a driver tests datasheet literacy and API judgment; debug this crash tests methodical hypothesis-testing.
The arc usually runs: phone screen (C basics + background), technical deep-dive (whiteboard + systems), practical (debug or take-home), behavioral (team fit). Prepare a story for each layer.
Interviewers hire for trajectory: showing how you reason through something unfamiliar beats reciting something memorized. Narrate, do not perform.

example.code:
INTERVIEW ARC
  Screen (30 min):  C fundamentals, your background, one bit-manipulation problem
  Deep dive (60):   whiteboard driver design + concurrency scenario
  Practical (60):   debug a failing board / analyze a crash dump
  Behavioral (30):  war stories — hardest bug, a disagreement, a deadline
example.walkthrough: This is the shape of most embedded interview loops. The screen filters for C fluency — if pointers and bit ops are not reflex, nothing else matters. The deep dive is where systems thinking shows: they watch how you decompose a driver design, not just whether you finish. The practical round tests debugging as a discipline — do you form hypotheses and test them, or flail? The behavioral round wants war stories with structure: situation, your action, the technical detail that proves you were there.

pitfalls: Preparing only trivia: reciting register names without ever having debugged a real board is transparent to experienced interviewers. Depth over breadth.
No war stories ready: tell me about your hardest bug with no answer prepared wastes your best material. Prepare three stories with technical depth.
Ignoring the behavioral round: embedded teams are small — can I debug next to this person at 2 AM is a real hiring criterion.
lessons.try_it: Write your three war stories now: hardest bug, a design decision you would defend, and a time you were wrong. Each gets: situation, your reasoning, the technical crux, the outcome.

lessons.title: Whiteboard C: Writing Clean Code Under Watch
concepts: Whiteboard code is judged on structure, not compilation: clear names, correct logic, handled edge cases. Nobody expects it to compile — everybody expects it to be readable.
State assumptions out loud: I will assume 32-bit little-endian and that the buffer is word-aligned. Stated assumptions are engineering; silent ones are bugs.
The bit-manipulation toolkit must be reflex: set/clear/toggle/test bit, extract field, count bits. Drill these until they are muscle memory — they appear in nearly every embedded screen.
Talk while you write: silence reads as stuck. Narrating first I will handle the null case, then the main loop shows structured thinking even before the code exists.

example.code:
/* set bit n, clear bit n, test bit n — the holy trinity */
#define BIT_SET(reg, n)    ((reg) |=  (1u << (n)))
#define BIT_CLEAR(reg, n)  ((reg) &= ~(1u << (n)))
#define BIT_TEST(reg, n)   (((reg) >> (n)) & 1u)
/* extract field: bits [hi:lo] */
#define FIELD_GET(reg, hi, lo) \
    (((reg) >> (lo)) & ((1u << ((hi)-(lo)+1)) - 1))
example.walkthrough: These four macros are the whiteboard survival kit. BIT_SET/CLR/TEST are the read-modify-write idioms interviewers expect without hesitation. FIELD_GET extracts an arbitrary bit field — shifting right to align the field, then masking to its width. Note the parenthesization: every macro argument and the whole body is wrapped, because an unparenthesized macro in an expression is a classic whiteboard trap the interviewer may probe. Write these from memory, correctly, and you have passed the C-fluency bar.

pitfalls: Shifting by the type width: 1u << 32 is undefined behavior. Interviewers probe this — know that shift counts must be less than the width.
Signed shift surprises: 1 << 31 on 32-bit int is UB (signed overflow). Use unsigned constants (1u, 1ul) in bit code, always.
Clever one-liners: a clever bit trick you cannot explain is worse than a clear loop. Clarity first — optimize only if asked.
lessons.try_it: On paper, write: toggle bit 7 of a register, extract bits [11:8] as a value, and count the set bits in a byte — without compiling. Then check each against the rules above.

lessons.title: Narrating Your Thinking: The Think-Aloud Protocol
concepts: Think-aloud is the highest-leverage interview skill: interviewers score your reasoning process, and they can only score what they hear. Silence is unscored.
The protocol: restate the problem, state assumptions, outline the approach before coding, narrate decisions as you make them, and verify at the end (let me check the edge cases).
Verbalize uncertainty honestly: I am not sure whether this peripheral clears on read — I would check the datasheet here is a senior answer. Bluffing is a junior tell.
Ask clarifying questions early: what is the clock speed? can the ISR block? Questions show you scope problems before solving them — exactly what the job requires.

example.code:
THINK-ALOUD SCRIPT (for any problem)
  1. Let me restate: we need X given Y.
  2. My assumptions: A, B. Should I verify any?
  3. Approach: first ___, then ___. Alternative would be ___.
  4. [work] I am choosing ___ because ___.
  5. Checking edge cases: null, zero, overflow, alignment.
  6. If I had the datasheet, I would confirm ___.
example.walkthrough: This script is a safety net for your mouth: when nerves blank your mind, step 1 gives you something true to say, and each step unlocks the next. Restating proves understanding; assumptions show engineering judgment; outlining before coding prevents the rambling-code trap. The edge-case check at step 5 is where embedded interviews are won — null pointers, zero lengths, overflow, and alignment are the exact cases interviewers watch for. Step 6 turns ignorance into process: not knowing is fine, knowing how you would find out is the skill.

pitfalls: Narrating every keystroke: now I am writing a for loop is noise. Narrate decisions and reasoning, not syntax.
Going silent when stuck: stuck-and-silent reads as giving up; stuck-and-talking (I am stuck on X — let me try reframing as Y) reads as resilience.
Never checking the interviewer's face: think-aloud is a dialogue. Pause for reactions — a nod means continue, a frown means revisit.
lessons.try_it: Record yourself solving a bit-manipulation problem while thinking aloud (phone voice memo). Listen back: count the decisions you verbalized vs the ones you made silently. Aim for 80 percent or more verbalized.

lessons.title: Systems Questions: From Pin to Cloud
concepts: Systems questions span the stack: trace a sensor reading from the pin to the cloud dashboard. They test whether you see the whole flow or only your layer.
The answering framework: enumerate the stages (transducer, ADC, driver, RTOS, radio stack, gateway, cloud, dashboard), then for each stage name the key mechanism and one failure mode.
Bottleneck reasoning: where would this break at 10x scale? — sample rate vs bus bandwidth, RAM vs buffering, radio duty cycle vs regulation, cloud ingest vs cost. Numbers beat hand-waving.
Trade-off fluency: polling vs interrupts, RTOS vs superloop, edge vs cloud processing. Every choice has a cost — name it, and say what would change your answer.

example.code:
PIN -> CLOUD TRACE (example: temperature sensor)
  pin:     analog voltage -> ADC samples at 1 kHz (aliasing? filter?)
  driver:  DMA double-buffer -> ISR half-transfer -> queue
  rtos:    sensor task filters -> comms task batches
  radio:   BLE notify 10 Hz -> gateway (duty cycle limits)
  cloud:   MQTT -> time-series DB -> dashboard (latency, retention)
example.walkthrough: This trace is the answer skeleton for any end-to-end question: each stage names the mechanism and the parenthetical names the failure mode or design question at that stage. Aliasing at the ADC, DMA overruns in the driver, queue sizing in the RTOS, duty-cycle regulation on the radio, retention cost in the cloud — mentioning one sharp detail per stage signals senior breadth. The interviewer will then drill into whichever stage interests them; your trace told them where the interesting problems are.

pitfalls: Staying in one layer: answering a systems question with only firmware detail misses the point. Touch every stage, even briefly.
No numbers: the radio sends data vs BLE notify at 10 Hz, 20-byte MTU, about 2 kbps goodput. Quantify — embedded is a quantitative discipline.
Forgetting failure modes: a trace without failure modes is a tour, not engineering. One failure mode per stage is the bar.
lessons.try_it: Trace your capstone sensor node end to end in 8 stages. For each: mechanism, one number (rate/size/latency), one failure mode. Time yourself — aim for under 5 minutes spoken.

lessons.title: Whiteboard Discipline: C Problems on the Clock
concepts: Timed whiteboard problems test fluency under pressure: 15-20 minutes, one C problem, narrated. The clock is part of the test — practice with a timer, not just on paper.
The winning structure: clarify (2 min), brute-force outline (3 min), clean implementation (8 min), edge-case sweep (3 min), complexity statement (1 min). Budget the minutes explicitly.
Write the signature first, then the loop invariant: this pointer always points at the last processed node — invariants keep pointer code correct when nerves fray.
Classic embedded whiteboard problems cluster: linked-list surgery, bit manipulation, string handling without libc, ring buffers, debouncing, fixed-point math. Drill the cluster, not random puzzles.

example.walkthrough: Three pointers, one invariant: prev always heads the reversed prefix. Each iteration saves head->next before overwriting it — the step beginners forget, losing the rest of the list. The loop ends when head is NULL, and prev is the new head. Edge cases to state aloud: empty list (returns NULL), single node (returns itself). Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space. Stating the invariant and the edge cases is what separates a pass from a strong hire.

pitfalls: Losing the next pointer: overwriting head->next before saving it orphans the list — the single most common whiteboard bug. Save first, always.
No NULL handling: dereferencing head without checking is an instant fail on embedded whiteboards. Guard first, loop second.
Silent type assumptions: int is 32 bits — state your assumptions about widths. Embedded interviewers notice.
lessons.try_it: Set a 15-minute timer. Whiteboard (paper, no compiler): remove all nodes with a given value from a singly linked list. Then do the edge-case sweep aloud.

lessons.title: Explain an RTOS in Five Minutes
concepts: The five-minute RTOS explanation is a staple: interviewers use it to test whether you understand the abstraction or just the API. Structure beats completeness.
The arc: the problem (superloop does not scale), the mechanism (tasks + scheduler + tick), the primitives (queues, semaphores, mutexes), the hazards (priority inversion, starvation), one war story.
Use one running example: the sensor node with sensor, comms, and supervisor tasks. Concrete beats abstract — the sensor task blocks on the data-ready semaphore lands harder than tasks synchronize.
End with judgment: when you would choose an RTOS vs bare metal — and the cost (RAM, complexity, determinism analysis). Opinions with reasons read as senior.

example.code:
5-MINUTE RTOS ARC
  0:00  A superloop breaks when timing gets complex — everything
        couples to everything.
  1:00  An RTOS gives each job its own task with its own stack;
        the scheduler always runs the highest-priority ready task.
  2:30  Tasks talk via queues (data), semaphores (events),
        mutexes (shared resources).
  3:30  The hazards: priority inversion — fixed by inheritance;
        starvation — fixed by design.
  4:30  On my sensor node: ... [your war story]
example.walkthrough: This script allocates the five minutes deliberately: problem framing first (why the RTOS exists), then the core mechanism in plain language, then the three primitives with their one-line purposes, then the two classic hazards with fixes — naming priority inversion unprompted signals depth. The final 30 seconds is yours: a real story from your experience makes the abstract concrete. Rehearse this aloud three times; the timing should feel natural, not recited.

pitfalls: API recitation: listing RTOS function names without explaining the model underneath. They want the mental model, not the manual.
Skipping the hazards: an RTOS explanation with no mention of inversion or starvation sounds like tutorial knowledge. Hazards prove experience.
No opinion on RTOS vs bare metal: always use an RTOS or never both read as junior. The senior answer names the trade-off and the threshold.
lessons.try_it: Record your five-minute RTOS explanation. Check: did you name the hazards? Did you include a real example? Was it under 5:30?

lessons.title: Reading a Crash Dump Like a Detective
concepts: Crash-dump questions test method: given stacked registers and a fault status, can you work backward to the cause? The dump is evidence; your job is the deduction chain.
The reading order: fault status register first (what kind of fault), stacked PC second (which instruction), then disassemble around it, then ask what made this address or content wrong.

Common signatures: PC in the weeds (stack corruption or bad function pointer), precise data abort on a peripheral address (clock gate off or wrong address), UsageFault on unaligned access (struct packing issue).
Always close the loop: the fix plus the prevention (assert, MPU region, code review check). Interviewers promote candidates who fix the class, not just the instance.

example.code:
CRASH DUMP                          DEDUCTION
  CFSR = 0x00008200                   bit 9: precise data bus error
  stacked PC = 0x08001234             objdump: LDR r0, [r1, #0x40]
  stacked R1 = 0x40013800             USART base... +0x40 = beyond
                                      peripheral region -> invalid address
  verdict: driver used wrong register offset; peripheral clock
  also suspect — but address is out of range regardless.
example.walkthrough: The CFSR's bit 9 names a precise data bus error — the CPU knows exactly which access faulted. The stacked PC disassembles to a load from [R1 + 0x40]; R1 holds a USART base address, and offset 0x40 is past the peripheral's register block — an invalid address, hence the bus error. The deduction chain is: fault type, faulting instruction, the bad address, why the address is bad (wrong offset constant in the driver). In the interview, narrate exactly this chain — each step is a scored reasoning move.

pitfalls: Jumping to the fix: it is a null pointer without reading the registers is guessing. The interview scores the chain, not the guess.
Ignoring the CFSR: the status register distinguishes bus errors from usage faults from memory-management faults — skipping it throws away the best clue.
No prevention story: fixing the offset without adding a static assert or review check leaves the bug class alive. Always name the prevention.
lessons.try_it: Take your last real (or deliberate) HardFault dump. Write the full deduction chain: CFSR, PC, disassembly, root cause, fix, prevention. Under one page.

lessons.title: Design a Driver: From Datasheet to API
concepts: Driver-design questions test API judgment: given a peripheral, design the interface others will use. Good APIs are small, hard to misuse, and hide hardware details.

The design flow: read the datasheet's functional description, list the operations users need (init, read, write, configure, sleep), choose the calling convention (blocking? callback? queue?), define error handling.
Layer the driver: a low-level register layer (static inline, tested against the datasheet) and a high-level API layer (the part users call). Never expose raw registers to application code.
Defend your choices: why blocking vs async, why this buffer size, how errors surface, what happens on invalid input. Every choice needs a reason you can state in one sentence.

example.walkthrough: The public API is four functions and one status enum — small enough to learn in a minute. Timeouts are explicit parameters, not hidden globals, so callers control blocking behavior. The status enum names the failure modes the hardware actually produces (timeout, framing error) instead of a bare bool. The comment draws the layering line: register manipulation lives in a separate low-level header, unit-testable without hardware. In the interview, presenting the API first and the internals second shows user-centered design thinking.

pitfalls: Exposing registers in the public API: register macros in the app-facing header couple every user to the hardware. Hide it.
No error paths: a driver API that cannot fail is a lie — every bus operation can time out. Design the errors before the happy path.
Blocking-only design with no timeout: a sensor that never responds hangs the caller forever. Every blocking call needs a timeout or a documented non-blocking alternative.
lessons.try_it: Design the API for an I2C temperature sensor driver: init, read_temperature (with timeout), sleep/wake, error enum. Write the header only — then defend each function to a partner.

simulations.title: The stack that ate the ISR
simulations.brief: A HardFault fires on every UART burst. The interviewer hands you the fault log and asks what the ISR is doing wrong.

steps.symptom: HardFault on UART receive. The ISR declares char buf[512] on the stack; the task stack is 1 KB and the ISR nests on it.
evidence: ISR stack = interrupted task stack (1024 B); buf[512] + call depth overflows it
options: Move the buffer to static storage (or shrink it) — ISRs get minimal stack by design
Increase the task stack to 8 KB
steps.explain: ISRs borrow the interrupted context's stack. Large locals in an ISR are the classic overflow; static or global buffers keep ISR stack tiny.

steps.symptom: Fault gone. Now received bytes occasionally corrupt when the main loop reads the buffer mid-ISR.
evidence: ISR writes rx_buf[head++]; main reads rx_buf[tail++] // no protection
options: Guard the shared indices: brief critical sections around the main-loop access, or a lock-free ring with single-owner indices
steps.explain: A preemptible reader and an ISR writer race on the indices. Brief critical sections (or a proper SPSC ring) make the handoff atomic.

steps.symptom: Stable on the bench. Prove it survives the worst case.
evidence: UART at max baud, all interrupts firing
options: Fill the stack with a canary pattern, run the worst-case interrupt storm, and verify the canary is intact
Test at half baud to be safe
steps.explain: Stack margin is measured, not assumed: paint canaries, run the worst case, check what survived.

simulations.debrief: ISR bugs are resource bugs: tiny ISR stacks, shared data that races, and margins you measure with canaries.

simulations.title: The flag the optimizer deleted
simulations.brief: The main loop polls a flag set by the ADC ISR. It works at -O0 and never fires at -O2. Explain it to the interviewer.

steps.symptom: Main loop polls data_ready set by the ADC ISR, but the loop never sees it at -O2. Works at -O0.
evidence: bool data_ready = false; // ISR sets true; while(!data_ready){}
loop compiled to while(true){} — the load was hoisted out
options: Declare the flag volatile so every access hits memory
Add a delay in the loop
steps.explain: The optimizer proved the flag 'never changes' inside the loop and deleted the load. volatile tells the compiler the value can change outside the visible flow.

steps.symptom: volatile added; the flag works. Now a 32-bit counter shared with the ISR reads torn values on this 16-bit core.
evidence: 16-bit data bus: 32-bit reads take two instructions
options: Protect the read with a brief critical section — volatile does not make multi-instruction access atomic
Read the counter twice and average
steps.explain: volatile guarantees visibility, not atomicity. On a 16-bit core a 32-bit read can straddle an ISR update; only a critical section closes that window.

steps.symptom: Counter fixed. The interviewer asks when volatile is NOT enough.
evidence: multi-field struct updated by ISR, read by main
options: When the shared state spans multiple words — use a critical section or a lock-free protocol; volatile alone cannot order them
steps.explain: volatile is per-access. Multi-word consistency needs atomicity across the whole update — critical sections, or sequence locks for readers.

simulations.debrief: volatile means 'this can change behind your back' — visibility, not atomicity. Shared multi-word state needs critical sections.

simulations.title: Priority inversion on the bus
simulations.brief: The high-priority control task misses its 1 ms deadline whenever the low-priority logger runs. Name the phenomenon and fix it.

steps.symptom: High-priority control task intermittently misses its 1 ms deadline when the low-priority logging task runs.
evidence: control task blocks 40 ms on spi_mutex held by logging task
options: Enable priority inheritance on the mutex so the holder temporarily runs at the blocker's priority
Raise the logging task to high priority
Make the control task poll instead of blocking
steps.explain: Classic unbounded priority inversion: medium tasks preempt the low holder indefinitely. Inheritance bounds the wait to one critical section.

steps.symptom: Inheritance enabled; deadlines hold. Now the interviewer asks about the alternative design.
evidence: three tasks share the SPI bus
options: A dedicated bus-manager task owning the SPI, with others sending requests via a queue — no shared mutex at all
Merge all three tasks into one
steps.explain: The server pattern eliminates the inversion class entirely: ownership serializes access through a queue, and priorities stay meaningful.

steps.symptom: Design chosen. How do you size the control task's stack?
options: Measure worst-case depth with canaries under max interrupt load, then add margin
Guess 4 KB like the last project
steps.explain: Stack sizing is empirical: worst-case call depth plus worst-case ISR nesting, measured with canaries, plus margin.

simulations.debrief: Priority inversion is a sharing problem: inherit priority to bound it, or restructure so nothing is shared.

simulations.title: The watchdog that kept biting
simulations.brief: The board resets every 90 seconds during firmware update. The watchdog is doing its job — your code is not. Fix the discipline.

steps.symptom: Board resets every 90 seconds during firmware update; the watchdog timeout is 2 s and erasing one flash sector takes 3 s.
evidence: reset cause: IWDG; always during sector erase
options: Feed the watchdog inside the erase polling loop — long operations must service it
steps.explain: The watchdog cannot distinguish 'busy' from 'hung'. Long operations feed it as they make progress; disabling it removes the safety net exactly when you need it.

steps.symptom: Feeding added. Now a hung I2C bus wedges the driver in a poll loop that keeps feeding the watchdog — no reset ever comes.
evidence: while(!done){ feed_wdg(); } // done never sets on bus hang
options: Feed from progress, not from spinning: only feed after verified forward progress, with a bounded retry count
steps.explain: Feeding without progress is a liveness lie. The watchdog must observe real advancement — bounded retries, then let it bite.

steps.symptom: Watchdog discipline fixed. The interviewer asks what the reset handler should do first.
options: Log the reset cause to retained RAM/flash before anything else — it is your only witness
steps.explain: The reset cause is volatile evidence. Capture it first, then initialize; post-mortems live or die on that first log line.

simulations.debrief: Watchdogs enforce liveness: feed on progress, bound your retries, and always log why you reset.

simulations.title: Whiteboard: the ring buffer
simulations.brief: Design a UART RX path: ISR produces bytes, task consumes. 40 minutes — talk tradeoffs out loud.

steps.symptom: Design a UART RX path: ISR produces bytes, task consumes. No heap, ISR budget under 2 us.
evidence: 115200 baud, no heap, ISR must stay under 2 us
options: Single-producer/single-consumer ring: ISR writes head, task reads tail, power-of-two size with mask indexing
Malloc a linked list per byte
Task polls the UART data register directly
steps.explain: SPSC rings are the canonical answer: no locks, no heap, O(1) ISR work. Power-of-two size turns modulo into a mask.

steps.symptom: Interviewer: how do head and tail stay consistent across the ISR boundary?
evidence: head written only by ISR, tail only by task
options: Single-owner indices plus volatile: each side writes its own index and reads the other's — no torn updates on aligned word reads
One shared counter with a mutex
Disable interrupts in the task for every byte
steps.explain: Single ownership removes the race: the ISR never touches tail, the task never touches head. volatile gives visibility; ownership gives atomicity.

steps.symptom: Last: the buffer fills up under load. Drop or block?
options: Count overruns and drop per policy — an ISR can never block, so overflow is a counted, reported event
Block the ISR until space frees
steps.explain: ISRs cannot wait, so overflow policy is a design decision: count it, report it, choose drop-oldest or drop-newest deliberately.

simulations.debrief: The ring-buffer answer is ownership: one writer, one reader, masked indices, and overflow as a counted event.

cheatsheet: Memory: stack (auto) / heap (manual, fragments) / static (.data/.bss, forever); never return stack pointers.
volatile = compiler may not assume; NOT atomic, NOT ordered, NOT thread-safe. MMIO + ISR flags only.
Alignment: compilers pad for it; serialize wire formats field-by-field; packed is non-portable.
UB to name: signed overflow, strict aliasing, use-after-free, null deref; -O0 vs -O2 divergence is the signature.
RTOS: tasks block, ISRs cannot; tickless idle saves battery; size stacks by watermark + margin.
IPC: queues buffer, notifications are light; FromISR variants in ISRs; mutexes inherit priority, semaphores do not.
Buses: UART async text, SPI fast full-duplex streaming, I2C slow multi-drop; mode/address agreement is manual.
Concurrency: mask interrupts briefly for ISR-shared data; SPSC rings need barriers (ordering!); multi-word reads tear.
Debug: HardFault -> stacked PC + CFSR/HFSR + BFAR/MMFAR; dead board -> power, clock, reset, attach-under-reset.
Power: budget first; sleep depth from wakeup economics; measure sleep current, do not trust typicals.
glossary: HardFault
Cortex-M fault escalated from a configurable fault; diagnosed via stacked registers.
Tickless idle
RTOS power mode suppressing the periodic tick during idle; wake on next deadline.
Priority inversion
High-priority task blocked behind low-priority holder; fixed by inheritance/ceiling.
SPSC
Single-producer/single-consumer: the tractable lock-free case (ring buffers).
Torn read
Multi-word read split across an update — half old, half new.
Strict aliasing
Compiler rule: different-type pointers are assumed not to alias; violating it is UB.
DMA
Direct Memory Access: peripheral-to-memory transfers without CPU involvement.
Watchdog
Hardware timer resetting the MCU unless kicked — the last-resort liveness guard.
Devicetree
Zephyr/Linux hardware description separating board config from drivers.
FMEA
Failure-mode analysis: enumerate, rank by likelihood x severity, mitigate the top.
